newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-MEPC says property may be too hot.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-MEPC says property may be too hot.

text.p: British property group MEPC's chief executive James Tuckey warned on Tuesday of the dangers of overheating in the sector but stressed his firm's own confidence.
"I think there is a feeling there are some signs the market may be overheating," Tuckey told Reuters after MEPC announced its interim results.
Tuckey was upbeat about MEPC's own prospects, with the markets moving in the group's favour.
"We certainly think it has got another 18-24 months to run," Tuckey said. "Its been an extremely active six months and we feel pretty comfortable with the outlook."
Earlier MEPC announced pre-tax profits before exceptionals for the six months to March 31 of 75.7 million stg, a rise of 13 percent on the same period the previous year.
But the group's swap termination provision of 73.2 million stg, announced in April, reduced the figure to just 2.5 million stg.

Tuckey said MEPC had come out of a busy six-month period including management changes and an overhaul of its finances. It has a development programme underway and a modest programme in the pipeline, he added.
He said the firm was acutely aware of the cyclical nature of the property market. "A correction will come and we need to be prepared."
MEPC has around 300 million stg of development expenditure still to be spent, with quite a large amount due in the next six months.
The lion's share of this was in Britain, with three different categories of schemes, spanning differing stages of development, underway.
Tuckey said MEPC was moving in the direction of leisure developments but this market was one where caution needed to be exercised.
In its results statement MEPC gave some indication of why it had ended merger talks with its smaller rival Hammerson in March.
It said the scale of potential cost savings and synergies was found to be small and the financial effect would have diluted MEPC's earnings per share and reduced its dividends.
Tuckey said MEPC had been in a "turbulent slipstream" in the months since the talks ended because of the speculation that followed.
But while he was not encouraging others to make approaches to MEPC, he said it would be negligent if he did not consider such moves.
Tuckey stressed MEPC was not talking to any other parties at the moment and he did not expect any such talks in the near future, although he could never discount the possibility altogether.

While there was plenty of talk of a "big deal" in the sector, Tuckey said he simply did not know if there was anything in the pipeline. But based on MEPC's talks with Hammerson, any likely cost savings were not great.
Tuckey said it was perhaps more correct to direct talk of rationalisation to the smaller property companies, where cost savings might be greater.
MEPC shares were quoted at 513 pence at 0845 GMT, down 2.5 pence.
